title: What Makes a Word Sound Funny? Sound Predicts Humor Beyond Frequency and Meaning
author: Mithun Thangaraj
paragraphs: This study asks whether the sounds of English words predict how funny they are rated, and whether this effect survives controls for word frequency, iconicity and meaning. Sound symbolism, the association between speech sounds and meanings, has been documented for size, shape and other perceptual qualities, and challenges the view that the link between sound and meaning is purely arbitrary. Humor offers a useful test case. Engelthaler and Hills (2018) collected humor ratings for 4,997 English words, and Kilpatrick and Flaksman (2025) showed that humorous words have higher phonemic surprisal and are more memorable despite their positive valence. However, funny words also tend to be rare and to carry distinctive meanings, so it is unclear whether specific sounds, rather than frequency or meaning, drive humor ratings.

We build XGBoost classifiers (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) on phoneme proportions and compare them with models that add lexical controls and meaning ratings, using nested, repeated cross-validation with permutation baselines. We also test a phonological feature model and word-position features, and use SHAP values (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) to identify which sounds push words toward funny or not funny.

All the data, the code, and the models are available {LINK}here{/LINK}. Data were processed in R (R Core Team, 2026) with the xgboost, caret (Kuhn, 2008), SHAPforxgboost and pROC (Robin et al., 2011) packages. Of the 42,222 entries in the source dataset, 4,852 words had humor ratings. Phoneme counts from the Carnegie Mellon University Pronouncing Dictionary (Weide, 1998) were corrected for a substring-counting error (only 37.1% of words originally summed to their phoneme length, 100% after correction; 50 of 50 randomly sampled words matched the dictionary exactly) and normalized by word length. Lexical controls were phonemic surprisal, iconicity (Winter et al., 2024), length and log10 SUBTLEX-US frequency (Brysbaert & New, 2009); meaning features were valence, arousal and dominance (Warriner et al., 2013) and concreteness (Brysbaert et al., 2014). Words were classified by a median split of humor ratings (N = 4,518) and by the top versus bottom 10% (N = 894). We compared a phoneme model (A), models adding surprisal, iconicity and length (B) and then frequency (C), a meaning model without phonemes (M; N = 4,438), the same model with phonemes (M+P), a model of 27 phonological features (F) and phonemes plus word-position features (A+Pos). All models were evaluated with stratified 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times, with hyperparameters tuned by inner 3-fold cross-validation inside each training fold only. Chance levels came from label permutations (200 for A and C, 100 for the other models), models sharing folds were compared with paired Wilcoxon tests on fold-level AUC, and a residual test asked whether phonemes predict the part of humor that a linear meaning model leaves unexplained (100 permutations).

Phonemes alone predicted humor above chance: model A reached AUC = 0.631 (SD = 0.023) for the median split and 0.785 (SD = 0.046) for the extreme groups, against permutation means of 0.50 (p = .005). Adding surprisal, iconicity and length, and then frequency, raised AUC to 0.717 and 0.879 (p < .001). Crucially, adding phonemes to the meaning model raised AUC from 0.735 to 0.751 (median split) and from 0.917 to 0.931 (extreme groups); M+P outperformed M in 45 and 46 of 50 folds (p < .001), and the gain held when NRC emotion associations were added (N = 3,362; 42 of 50 folds, p < .001). In the residual test, phonemes predicted humor left unexplained by meaning and frequency (cross-validated R² = 0.063, r = 0.25), whereas shuffled phonemes did not (R² = -0.001; p = .010). SHAP directions in M+P closely matched the phoneme-only model (rho = 0.91): /u/, /ɡ/ and /ŋ/ pushed words toward funny and /eɪ/, /ɛ/, /θ/ and /aɪ/ toward not funny (Table 1). Word-position features added AUC 0.011 (p < .001), with word-final /i/ the strongest cue, and words spelled -le were rated funnier than other words (d = 0.54). The phonological feature model reached AUC = 0.621 (phonemes: 0.631); high, central and back vowels and velar and labial consonants pushed toward funny, while front, diphthongal and mid vowels and alveolar consonants pushed toward not funny (Table 2).

Sound therefore contributes to humor ratings beyond word frequency, iconicity and meaning, although the contribution is modest: frequency, iconicity and meaning remain the strongest predictors, and phonemes account for 30% of the M+P model's SHAP importance. Phonemic surprisal correlated positively with humor (r = 0.08), in line with Kilpatrick and Flaksman (2025), but removing it from model C did not lower AUC (p = .217 and p = .454), and higher-surprisal words were rarer (r = -0.16), suggesting that part of the earlier surprisal effect reflects word frequency. Meaning ratings do not capture taboo senses, phoneme proportions ignore stress and order, and overlapping folds make the Wilcoxon p-values optimistic. Overall, specific sounds make English words funnier, and cross-validated machine learning with permutation baselines can separate this effect from frequency and meaning.
